title: How a promise becomes a contract
summary: A contract is a promise the law will enforce, and it forms only when certain elements are present: offer, matching acceptance, something given in exchange, an intention to be bound and terms certain enough to enforce. Conditions then decide when the obligations bite. This lesson explains both, in general common-law terms, with two developer examples.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a contract is not a document; it is a set of promises the law will enforce. It can be formed by an email chain or a handshake, and a thick signed document can still fail to form one. Know the elements, and you will know when you are bound before your lawyer has to tell you.

Recall

Q. From last week: which layer prevails when a by-law conflicts with a valid statute?

A. Generally the statute, because the by-law is made under delegated power and is valid only within it. Check first that the statute applies to the site and is in force.

Q. From the money checkpoint: what four tags travel with every number you hand over?

A. Its type, meaning fact, assumption or opinion; its source; its date; and its sensitivity or range.

Q. From the owner accounting week: what is a capitalised cost?

A. A cost recorded as part of the asset on the balance sheet, such as construction and interest during construction, rather than as an expense in the year it is paid.

Why this matters

Development is a chain of contracts: land purchase, consultants, construction, loans, leases and sales. Most disputes in that chain are not about what was promised but about whether a promise was made at all, and when it took effect. A developer who can recognise the moment a contract forms can stop himself from being bound early, and can bind the other side when it matters. Everything below is general and conceptual, in the common-law tradition; the rules differ by jurisdiction, so verify against the primary source before you rely on them.

The elements of formation

Plain English first. Someone proposes a deal; the other side says yes to exactly that deal; each gives something; both mean it to be legally binding; and the deal is clear enough that a court could tell what each must do.

The professional framing, element by element.

  • Offer. A proposal made with the intention that, if accepted, it will bind. An invitation to negotiate, such as a property listing or "we'd consider around $2,000,000," is usually not an offer.
  • Acceptance. Unqualified agreement to the offer's terms. A reply that changes a term is commonly treated as a counter-offer, which rejects the original and puts a new offer on the table.
  • Consideration. In common-law systems, each side must give or promise something of value in exchange. A bare promise with nothing in return is generally not enforceable unless made in a special form, such as a deed under seal. Civil-law systems approach this differently.
  • Intention to create legal relations. Commercial dealings are usually presumed to be intended as binding unless the parties clearly say otherwise, for example with "subject to contract."
  • Certainty. The essential terms must be agreed or capable of being worked out. An "agreement to agree" the price later is commonly unenforceable.

Some contracts, including many for the sale of land, must also be in writing and signed to be enforceable. That requirement varies by place; verify it locally.

Worked example one: the email chain

Hypothetical. You email a landowner: "I offer $2,000,000 for your 2,000 square metre lot, closing in 90 days, deposit $100,000." She replies: "Agreed, but closing in 60 days." You reply: "Fine, 60 days works." Where is the contract?

Your first email looks like an offer: it names the property, price, closing and deposit. Her reply changes the closing date, so it is a counter-offer, not an acceptance, and your original offer is gone. Your second email accepts her counter-offer without qualification. Subject to any requirement for land contracts to be in a particular written and signed form, you may now have a binding deal at $2,000,000 with a 60-day close, though you never signed a document and never intended to commit before your diligence. That is how developers get bound by accident.

The control is a phrase at the top of every pre-contract email: "This is not an offer capable of acceptance. No contract will exist until a formal agreement is signed by both parties."

Say that out loud now.

Conditions: when the promise bites

Plain English: a contract can exist today while some obligations wait for an event.

The professional framing. A condition precedent is an event that must happen before an obligation, or sometimes the whole contract, takes effect: financing approved, rezoning granted, satisfactory environmental report. A condition subsequent ends an obligation if an event occurs later. Conditions can be drafted in favour of one party, who can then waive them, or both. A well-drafted condition states the event, the standard for satisfying it, who decides, the deadline, how notice is given, and what happens if it fails. Courts in many places will also expect a party to make reasonable efforts to satisfy a condition, not sabotage it.

Worked example two: the financing condition

Hypothetical round numbers. You agree to buy land for $2,000,000 with a $100,000 deposit, "conditional on the buyer obtaining financing." Sixty days later rates have risen and you would rather not buy. Can you walk away?

It depends on the drafting, which is exactly the problem. "Obtaining financing" on what terms? By when? Decided by whom? If a lender offered $1,300,000 at a rate you dislike, has the condition been met? A vague condition invites a dispute over the $100,000 deposit, and possibly over the whole $2,000,000 obligation.

The better version: "Conditional, for the sole benefit of the buyer, on the buyer receiving by 5 p.m. on [date] a written loan commitment of at least $1,300,000 on terms satisfactory to the buyer in its sole discretion. The buyer will make reasonable efforts to obtain it. If the buyer does not give written notice of satisfaction or waiver by that time, the agreement ends and the deposit is returned in full." Every phrase answers one of the six questions above. Whether "sole discretion" language is upheld varies; that is a question for local counsel.

How the best do it

Large, experienced owners and contractors generally do not draft contracts from scratch. They work from recognised standard forms and their own approved precedents, keep a list of clauses they will not change without senior sign-off, and track every condition and notice deadline in a register owned by a named person. The point is not paperwork; it is that the dangerous moments, formation, condition deadlines and notices, are caught by a system rather than by memory. A small developer can copy this with a one-page precedent for pre-contract emails and a spreadsheet of every condition date in every live deal.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is being bound before you mean to be, through an email, a signed letter of intent or conduct that treats the deal as done. The control is a standing rule: every pre-contract communication carries an express statement that it is not an offer and that nothing binds until a formal agreement is signed, and you never act on a deal, by paying, announcing or starting work, before it is signed. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where the land sits.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking a signature is what makes a contract. Signatures matter, especially for land, but conduct and correspondence can form a contract without one, and a signed document can still be unenforceable if a term is too uncertain. Read for the elements, not for the signature block.

Callback

In week 2 you learned about go/no-go gates: fixed points where you decide against written criteria. A condition precedent is a gate written into a contract. If the financing, rezoning or environmental gate is not met by the stated date, the contract lets you stop without loss. Draft your conditions to match your gates, and your project controls and your legal rights become the same thing.

Recap

A contract forms when an offer is accepted without changes, each side gives something, both intend to be bound and the terms are certain. A counter-offer kills the original offer. Conditions decide when obligations bite, and each one should state the event, the standard, who decides, the deadline, the notice and the consequence.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on a deal announced as agreed in principle, and the multi-billion-dollar verdict that followed.
checklist: Put a not-an-offer statement on every pre-contract email and letter.
Check whether a reply changes any term; if it does, it is a counter-offer.
Confirm what something of value each side is giving.
Never leave the price or another essential term to be agreed later.
Check whether a land contract must be in writing and signed where the land sits.
Draft each condition with event, standard, decider, deadline, notice and consequence.
Log every condition deadline in a register with a named owner.
head: Field checklist
speak: A contract is a set of promises the law will enforce, not a document. In common-law systems it forms when there is an offer, an acceptance that matches it exactly, consideration given by each side, an intention to be legally bound, and terms certain enough to enforce. A reply that changes a term is a counter-offer that kills the original, and an email chain can form a contract without a signature, subject to any rule that land contracts must be in signed writing. Conditions decide when obligations bite. A condition precedent must happen before an obligation takes effect, such as financing or rezoning. Each condition should say what event, what standard, who decides, by when, how notice is given and what happens if it fails. My rule: every pre-contract message says it is not an offer, and I never act on a deal before it is signed.
terms: Consideration — something of value given or promised by each party in exchange, generally needed for a common-law contract to bind.
Counter-offer — a reply that changes the terms of an offer, rejecting it and making a new offer in its place.
Condition precedent — an event that must occur before an obligation, or the contract itself, takes effect.

hostile.q: The landowner's lawyer says your emails formed a binding contract at 2 million and demands you close. Did they?
hostile.a: Possibly, which is why I have stopped all further correspondence and asked our lawyer to review the chain against the formation rules and any writing requirement for land contracts where the site is. My emails offered a price, she countered on closing, and I replied agreeing. If that formed a contract, our position will rest on the requirement for signed writing and on the conditions. From now on every pre-contract email carries a not-an-offer statement, and I will not discuss terms again until the lawyer has advised.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: Pennzoil and Texaco: the agreement in principle that cost billions
summary: In 1984 Pennzoil and the main Getty Oil shareholders announced an agreement in principle; days later Texaco bought Getty instead. A Texas jury in 1985 found the first deal was binding and returned a verdict of more than ten billion dollars against Texaco, which later sought bankruptcy protection and settled. The case is the clearest lesson in what a preliminary agreement can bind.
rule: Rule 20: Every letter of intent I sign or receive states, in its first paragraph, which clauses bind and which do not; I never announce, act on or let anyone treat a deal as agreed until the definitive agreement is signed, and I never step into a deal without written confirmation that no one else holds a binding agreement.
body:
Mr Shabazz, whether a preliminary agreement binds is decided by what the parties said and did, not by what they meant to sign later. Pennzoil against Texaco turned that question into one of the largest jury verdicts in history. Cole sits beside me today, because the lesson is as much about the paper trail as the law.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what are the elements of contract formation?

A. An offer, an acceptance that matches it, consideration from each side, an intention to be legally bound, and terms certain enough to enforce. Some contracts, including many for land, must also be in signed writing.

Q. From the money checkpoint: what is Rule 18?

A. Every month I reconcile reported profit to the cash actually collected and paid; if the gap widens two months running, I stop advancing money until the cash explains the profit.

Q. From the owner accounting week: why does reporting matter to a lender?

A. Because the lender relies on your reports to decide whether to keep funding. Reports that are late, inconsistent or optimistic cost you credibility, and credibility is what a lender lends on when things go wrong.

Why this matters

Developers sign preliminary documents constantly: letters of intent, term sheets, heads of terms, memoranda of understanding. Each one is a moment when you may be bound to the other side, or when a third party may already be bound to someone else. This case shows both risks at full scale. The facts below come from public reporting of the trial and later proceedings; verify the specifics against primary sources before you cite them.

Step 1: Timeline

Around the turn of 1984, Pennzoil sought to acquire a large stake in Getty Oil. In early January 1984 it reached terms with the two largest Getty shareholders, a family trust and the J. Paul Getty Museum, and the Getty Oil board voted to approve a plan on those terms. A press release described an agreement in principle, and lawyers began drafting the definitive merger documents. Within days, Texaco offered a higher price, and the Getty interests agreed to sell to Texaco instead. Pennzoil sued Texaco in a Texas state court, claiming Texaco had induced Getty to break a binding contract. In November 1985 a jury found that a binding agreement had existed and that Texaco had interfered with it, and returned a verdict of more than ten billion dollars including punitive damages. The award was later reduced on appeal. In April 1987 Texaco filed for bankruptcy protection, in part because of the difficulty of posting security while it appealed, and the parties settled later that year for about three billion dollars.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions matter. The Getty side approved and announced a deal described as an agreement in principle without stating clearly that nothing would bind until definitive documents were signed. Texaco chose to make a competing offer to parties who had just announced an agreement with someone else, relying on assurances and indemnities from the sellers rather than on certainty that no binding contract existed. And Pennzoil chose to sue the new buyer rather than only the sellers.

Step 3: Assumptions

Everyone involved assumed the deal was not final until the merger agreement was signed, because that is how large deals usually work. That assumption was the whole case. The jury was asked whether the parties had intended to be bound when they agreed the terms, and on the evidence before it, including the board vote, the handshakes and the press release, it decided they had. A shared industry assumption is not a term of the contract unless someone writes it down.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Cole's view from the auditor's chair. The sellers had every reason to take the higher price. Texaco had every reason to move fast, before the first deal was papered. Advisers on both sides were paid to close a deal, not to slow one down by asking whether an earlier one already bound. And no one's incentive was to write a clear, short sentence saying "this is not binding," because that sentence would have weakened the announcement each side wanted to make.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

A board vote approving specific terms. A public announcement of an agreement. Work already started on definitive documents. Any one of these can be argued either way. Together they are exactly the evidence a court looks at when it asks whether parties intended to be bound. A buyer arriving days later should treat that set of facts as a red flag that someone may already hold a contract.

Step 6: Point of no return

For Texaco, the point of no return was signing with sellers who had announced an agreement with Pennzoil days before, without either a clear public statement that the first deal was non-binding or the first buyer's release. Once it did, it had stepped into the middle of a possible contract, and the size of the deal set the size of the exposure.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was ambiguity about whether a preliminary agreement bound, created by conduct and announcement rather than resolved in writing, and then acted on by a third party that treated the ambiguity as someone else's problem.

The developer's version

Hypothetical round numbers. A landowner signs a one-page letter of intent with Buyer A at $2,000,000, announces it to the neighbours, and lets Buyer A's surveyor onto the site. Two weeks later you offer $2,300,000. The owner says, "Don't worry, the letter wasn't binding," and offers you an indemnity. If a court later finds the letter did bind, Buyer A may claim against the owner for breach and, in some systems, against you for inducing it. Buyer A's claim might be the profit it expected on the site. If its residual analysis showed a $600,000 margin, that is the order of magnitude of your exposure, plus legal costs that could reach six figures, against an owner's indemnity that is only as good as the owner's assets.

The prevention is cheap: read Buyer A's letter yourself, with your lawyer, and get either a signed release from Buyer A or written confirmation, supported by the document, that it was expressly non-binding.

What would have changed the outcome

One sentence in the original announcement and in the board approval: "No party is bound until a definitive merger agreement is signed by all parties." That sentence would have cost nothing and would very likely have removed the case. For Texaco, one more step: refusing to proceed without the first bidder's release or an unambiguous written basis that no binding agreement existed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming that everyone understands a preliminary document the way you do. Courts decide on words and conduct, not on what is customary. The control is Rule 20: the first paragraph of every letter of intent lists which clauses bind, such as confidentiality, exclusivity and costs, and states that everything else binds only on signature of a definitive agreement.

The beginner's mistake

Relying on an indemnity from a seller to protect you from a prior buyer. An indemnity moves risk only as far as the indemnifier's ability to pay. Check whether the prior agreement binds; do not insure against it with a promise.

Rule 20

Every letter of intent I sign or receive states, in its first paragraph, which clauses bind and which do not; I never announce, act on or let anyone treat a deal as agreed until the definitive agreement is signed, and I never step into a deal without written confirmation that no one else holds a binding agreement.

Callback

In week 17, Rule 17 said to reverse every price before you pay it. Pennzoil adds a legal step to that diligence: before you pay any price, confirm that the asset is actually free to sell to you. A bargain that someone else already holds under contract is not a bargain; it is a lawsuit with a price attached.

Recap

An agreement in principle, a board vote and an announcement were enough for a jury to find a binding deal, and a second buyer that stepped in faced a verdict of more than ten billion dollars before the case settled. The root cause was ambiguity left in writing and in conduct. Rule 20 removes it.

Next: JAX, on what a condition, a deposit and an exclusivity period are actually worth in money.
checklist: Open every letter of intent with a list of binding and non-binding clauses.
State that nothing else binds until a definitive agreement is signed.
Do not announce, pay, mobilise or publicise a deal before definitive signature.
Ask any seller whether another party holds a letter of intent or agreement.
Read any prior letter of intent with your lawyer before you make an offer.
Obtain the prior party's release or clear written proof the earlier document was non-binding.
Never rely on a seller's indemnity alone to cover a prior buyer's claim.
head: Field checklist
speak: In January 1984 Pennzoil reached terms with the main Getty Oil shareholders, the Getty board approved, and a press release announced an agreement in principle while lawyers drafted the merger documents. Days later Texaco offered more and the Getty interests sold to Texaco. Pennzoil sued Texaco for interfering with a binding contract. In November 1985 a Texas jury agreed that a binding deal had existed and returned a verdict of more than ten billion dollars. The award was reduced on appeal, Texaco sought bankruptcy protection in 1987, and the case settled for about three billion. The root cause was ambiguity: conduct and an announcement suggested a deal, and nothing in writing said it was not binding. My rule: every letter of intent says in its first paragraph what binds and what does not, I never treat a deal as done before signature, and I never step into a deal without confirming no one else holds one.
terms: Agreement in principle — agreement on the main terms of a deal, whose binding force depends on the parties' words and conduct.
Tortious interference — a legal wrong committed by knowingly inducing someone to break a contract with another party.
Definitive agreement — the full, final contract that the parties intend to govern the deal, as opposed to a preliminary document.

hostile.q: The seller has a letter of intent with another buyer but says it is non-binding and will indemnify you. Why are you delaying the purchase?
hostile.a: Because an indemnity is only as strong as the seller's assets, and the question of whether the earlier letter binds is decided by its words and by what the parties did, not by what the seller tells us now. Our lawyer is reading that letter today. If it clearly says it is non-binding, or the other buyer signs a release, we proceed this week. If not, we do not sign, because the exposure is the other buyer's lost profit plus costs.

title: What a condition, a deposit and exclusivity are worth
summary: Contract terms have prices. A condition is a right to walk away, a deposit is money at risk, and an exclusivity period is time bought from the seller. This lesson puts a dollar value on each using expected loss, shows how much more you can rationally pay for a conditional deal, and adds what at-risk deposits mean for a personal balance sheet.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every clause in a land contract has a price, even when no one names it. A condition is the right to walk away, a deposit is money you agree to lose if you do, and exclusivity is time you buy from the seller. Price each one, and you will know what to trade and what to hold.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what is Rule 20?

A. Every letter of intent states in its first paragraph which clauses bind and which do not; nothing is treated as agreed until the definitive agreement is signed; and I never step into a deal without written confirmation that no one else holds a binding agreement.

Q. From the money checkpoint: what is a ceiling price?

A. The highest price at which a deal exactly meets its required return, with no cushion. You offer below the ceiling of the stress case.

Q. From the owner accounting week: why are deposits paid on land usually recorded as an asset rather than an expense?

A. Because they are part of the cost of acquiring the land, or refundable claims, not costs of running the business. They become an expense only if they are lost.

Why this matters

Sellers often offer a lower price for an unconditional deal, or a higher price for a long, conditional one. Without a way to price conditions, you will either pay too much for comfort or give away protection to save a small amount. The money version of contract law is simple: what does each right save you in the cases where you need it, multiplied by how likely those cases are?

The condition as insurance

Plain English: a condition lets you leave if a bad fact turns up. Its value is the loss it saves you in the bad case, times the chance of the bad case.

The professional framing is expected loss: the probability-weighted cost of an outcome. Compare the expected loss with the condition and without it.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. You agree to buy land for $2,000,000. Diligence might reveal a problem, contaminated fill or a buried service, that makes the land worth only $1,400,000. You estimate a 25 percent chance of that, an honest guess you should write down with its reasoning. Diligence itself costs $50,000 either way.

Unconditional: in the bad case you must close and you lose $600,000 of value. Expected loss is 25 percent of $600,000, which is $150,000, plus the $50,000 of diligence.

Conditional on satisfactory diligence: in the bad case you walk away and lose only the $50,000 diligence cost, and your deposit is returned. Expected loss from the bad case is close to zero beyond the diligence.

So the condition is worth about $150,000 to you. If the seller offers $1,900,000 unconditional or $2,000,000 conditional, the $100,000 discount is less than the $150,000 the condition saves on your own estimate. Take the conditional deal at the higher price. If the discount were $200,000, the unconditional deal would be cheaper on expected value, though only if you could survive the bad case, which is a separate question about your balance sheet.

Say that out loud now.

The deposit as money at risk

Plain English: a deposit shows commitment, and it is the amount the seller keeps if you default.

The professional framing. Deposits are often staged: a small refundable deposit on signing, a larger one when conditions are waived, sometimes more at later milestones. The key date is waiver, because that is when the deposit typically becomes non-refundable and your risk changes from "lose the diligence cost" to "lose the deposit, and possibly more." Whether a seller can keep a large deposit, or claim beyond it, depends on the contract wording and local law on forfeiture and penalties; tomorrow LEX covers remedies.

Worked example two. The seller proposes a $200,000 deposit, non-refundable from signing, with a 60-day diligence period. You propose $50,000 refundable on signing and a further $150,000 on waiver. On the seller's terms, if diligence fails, you lose $200,000 plus $50,000 of costs. On yours, you lose $50,000 of costs. Using the 25 percent chance from above, the seller's structure adds an expected $50,000 of cost to you. That figure is your guide to what a staged deposit is worth in a trade: you might accept a slightly higher price, or a shorter diligence period, in exchange for keeping the deposit refundable until waiver.

Exclusivity as bought time

An exclusivity clause, sometimes called a no-shop, stops the seller marketing to others for a period. It is one of the clauses a letter of intent usually makes binding, and it has a cost to the seller, who loses other buyers' interest. Sellers often ask for a non-refundable fee for it. Price it against what the time is worth to you: if 90 days of exclusivity lets you complete diligence that would otherwise be wasted when someone else outbids you, and you are spending $50,000 on that diligence, paying a $20,000 fee may be cheap. If you could do the diligence in 30 days, buy 30, not 90.

One more pricing check: carrying cost. A longer conditional period is not free to you either. If your team, consultants and overhead cost about $15,000 a month while the deal is live, a 90-day period costs about $45,000 against $15,000 for 30 days. A long condition you do not need can cost more than the protection it adds, so match the period to the work you actually have to do, and put that work on a schedule before you sign.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: a non-refundable deposit is not just a project cost; on your personal balance sheet it is cash already at risk on one outcome. Add up every deposit across your live deals that would be lost if you defaulted, plus any personal guarantee behind them, and compare that total with your liquidity floor. If one bad month could cost more than the floor, you are over-committed, however good each deal looks alone. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Monthly thread: personal brand

Your reputation in a land market is built mostly from how you handle these clauses. A buyer who waives conditions on the stated date, does not invent problems to retrade the price, and returns diligence reports promptly when he walks becomes the buyer sellers and brokers call first.

The opposite reputation spreads just as fast. Use conditions for what they are for, protection against real findings, and say so plainly when you walk: "We found contamination that the price cannot absorb; here is the report." That sentence costs you nothing and keeps the next deal open.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing protection by feel, which usually means paying too much for comfort when you are nervous and giving it away when you are excited. The control is to write down, for every live deal, the probability and size of the main bad outcome, and to use expected loss to decide what each condition, deposit structure and exclusivity period is worth before you negotiate.

The beginner's mistake

Treating expected value as the only test. An unconditional deal can have a better expected value and still be wrong if the bad case would sink you. Always ask two questions: what is it worth on average, and can I survive the worst case?

Callback

In the law-and-courts week, Roman priced a dispute by its expected value: probability of winning times the award, less costs. Today is the same arithmetic used earlier and more cheaply. A condition that lets you walk away is a dispute you never have to fight.

Recap

A condition is worth the loss it avoids times the chance of needing it. A deposit is money at risk, and the waiver date is when the risk changes. Exclusivity is time, worth what it saves you in wasted diligence. Price each before you trade it, and check that your total at-risk deposits stay inside your liquidity floor.

Next: LEX, on breach and remedies: what you can get when the other side fails to perform.
checklist: Write the probability and size of each deal's main bad outcome.
Value each condition as expected loss avoided.
Compare any price discount for an unconditional deal with the condition's value.
Keep deposits refundable until the waiver date where you can.
Buy only as much exclusivity as your diligence genuinely needs.
Total every at-risk deposit and guarantee against your liquidity floor.
When you walk, say why and share the finding.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every clause has a price. A condition is the right to walk away, and it is worth the loss it saves times the chance you need it. If there is a 25 percent chance diligence shows land worth 1.4 million instead of 2 million, a diligence condition saves an expected 150,000, so paying 100,000 more for a conditional deal is rational. A deposit is money at risk, and the key date is waiver, when it usually becomes non-refundable. Keeping it refundable until then can be worth tens of thousands in expected value, which tells me what I can trade for it. Exclusivity is time bought from the seller, worth what it saves in wasted diligence, so I buy only the days I need. Expected value is not the only test: I also ask whether I can survive the worst case, and I keep total at-risk deposits inside my liquidity floor.
terms: Expected loss — the cost of a bad outcome multiplied by its probability, used to price protection.
Waiver date — the date by which a buyer must confirm or give up its conditions, often when a deposit becomes non-refundable.
Exclusivity — a seller's promise not to market or negotiate with others for a set period.

hostile.q: The seller will knock 100,000 off if you go unconditional today. You are leaving money on the table. Why?
hostile.a: Because on our own estimate there is about a 25 percent chance diligence finds a problem that takes 600,000 off the land's value, so the diligence condition is worth roughly 150,000 to us, more than the discount. And if that bad case happened unconditionally, it would hit our liquidity floor. We will pay the full price with a 45-day diligence condition, or we can discuss a shorter period in exchange for a smaller discount.

title: When the other side fails: breach and remedies
summary: A breach is a failure to do what the contract requires, and the law's main answer is money: damages that put the innocent party where performance would have put it, limited by mitigation and foreseeability. Land contracts add specific performance, and well-drafted contracts add liquidated damages, deposits and termination rights. This lesson explains each in general terms, with two worked examples.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when a contract is broken, the law usually does not force the promise to be kept; it puts a price on the failure. Knowing how that price is set, and the few cases where a court will order performance instead, tells you what your contract is really worth before anything goes wrong.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: how do you value a condition?

A. As expected loss avoided: the loss it saves in the bad case times the probability of that case. Then check separately that you could survive the worst case without it.

Q. From the money checkpoint: what is the difference between a fact and a forecast in what you hand over?

A. A fact is true or false now. A forecast is about the future and generally carries an implied promise that you honestly hold it and have reasonable grounds. A false fact that induces a contract can support a misrepresentation claim; a forecast without basis can too.

Q. From the owner accounting week: what is accrual accounting?

A. Recording revenue when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, rather than when cash moves.

Why this matters

Every remedy clause in your contracts, every deposit, every liquidated damages figure and every termination right is a decision about what happens on the bad day. If you do not understand the default rules, you cannot tell whether your contract improves them or quietly gives them away. Concepts only, in the common-law tradition; the details vary by jurisdiction, so verify against the primary source before you rely on them. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed where the contract will be enforced.

What counts as breach

Plain English: the other side did not do what it promised, did it badly or late, or made clear it will not do it.

The professional framing. A breach can be actual, a failure to perform when due, or anticipatory, a clear statement or conduct before the due date showing a party will not perform. Breaches differ in seriousness. A minor breach usually gives a right to damages but not to end the contract. A serious breach, often called material or repudiatory, may allow the innocent party to terminate as well as claim damages. Whether a breach is serious enough is a judgement, which is why contracts often list specific events that allow termination and say how notice must be given. And where a contract says time is of the essence for a date, such as closing, missing it may itself be serious enough to end the deal.

Damages: the default remedy

The general aim of contract damages is to put the innocent party in the position it would have been in if the contract had been performed. Two limits matter in practice. Mitigation: the innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce its loss and cannot recover what it could reasonably have avoided. Remoteness: losses are generally recoverable only if they were reasonably foreseeable as a likely result of the breach when the contract was made, or arose from special circumstances both parties knew about.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. A seller agrees to sell you land for $2,000,000, then refuses to close because land values have risen. Similar land now costs $2,300,000. You buy a comparable site at that price and spend $30,000 on new diligence. Your basic loss is the $300,000 difference in price plus the $30,000 of wasted costs, about $330,000. If you also claim the profit you expected to make on the building, that claim faces the remoteness and certainty tests: a court may be sceptical of a forecast development profit, however carefully modelled. The tighter your evidence, the more of it you are likely to recover.

Say that out loud now.

Specific performance: when money is not enough

For most contracts, money is the answer. Land has traditionally been treated as unique, so many courts will consider ordering a defaulting seller to complete the sale, a remedy called specific performance. It is discretionary, not automatic: a court may refuse it if the buyer delayed, behaved unfairly, was not ready to close itself, or if damages would be adequate. Some courts have become more willing to treat investment land as replaceable, which weakens the argument. For a developer, the practical point is that specific performance is a possibility to be argued for with evidence that the site is genuinely unique to your project, not a certainty to rely on.

Deposits, liquidated damages and penalties

Contracts can set the price of breach in advance. A deposit is commonly forfeitable by a defaulting buyer. Liquidated damages are a sum agreed in advance as the compensation for a defined breach, such as a daily amount for late completion of a building. Courts in many common-law systems will enforce such a sum if it is a genuine attempt to estimate loss or protects a legitimate interest proportionately, but may refuse to enforce a sum that is extravagant and serves only to punish, which is called a penalty. Where the line sits varies by jurisdiction and has moved over time; verify against current law.

Worked example two. You sell a finished unit for $500,000 with a $50,000 deposit. The buyer defaults. You remarket and, after three months, sell for $460,000, spending $15,000 on extra carrying and selling costs. Your loss is the $40,000 price difference plus $15,000, which is $55,000. If the contract and local law let you keep the $50,000 deposit, you may also claim the further $5,000, depending on the wording. If you had refused a reasonable offer of $480,000 in the first month while holding out for full price, a court might find you failed to mitigate and reduce your claim by the $20,000 you could have avoided. A 10 percent deposit protected most, but not all, of the loss.

Termination and notice

Terminating a contract is a serious step. If you terminate without a right to do so, you may become the party in breach. Most commercial contracts set out a process: notice of default, a cure period, then a right to terminate, with notices to be given in a stated form to a stated address. Follow it exactly. In construction and finance documents, missing a notice deadline can cost you the right entirely; that is a later week on time bars.

Breach is not the only way out

Do not confuse breach with the other routes out of a contract. A misrepresentation that induced the contract, the subject of the money checkpoint, may allow the contract to be set aside, called rescission, which aims to put both sides back where they were before it was made rather than where performance would have put them. A failed condition precedent may end the contract with no breach by anyone. Each route has different consequences for deposits and costs, so the first question after anything goes wrong is which route you are actually on.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming your remedy is whatever feels fair. Remedies are set by the contract and the default rules, limited by mitigation, foreseeability and the penalty rule, and enforced only through a process that costs time and money. The control is to read every remedy, deposit and termination clause before you sign, and ask: if the other side fails tomorrow, what exactly do I get, how fast, and through what steps?

The beginner's mistake

Terminating in anger. A furious email saying "the deal is off" can itself be a repudiation if your right to terminate was not yet clear. When the other side breaches, stop, document, take advice, and act through the notice process the contract sets out.

Callback

In week 3 you met loss aversion: losses feel larger than equal gains. After a breach, that feeling pushes you to refuse reasonable offers and chase full recovery. The mitigation rule works directly against that instinct: the law expects you to cut your loss reasonably, and it will not pay for the part you could have avoided.

Recap

Breach can be actual or anticipatory, minor or serious. Damages aim to put you where performance would have, limited by mitigation and foreseeability. Specific performance of land contracts is possible but discretionary. Deposits and liquidated damages set the price of breach in advance, within the penalty rule. Terminate only with a clear right, by the contract's process.

Next: Roman, working backward from the worst day to the deposit and conditions you need.
checklist: Identify which events in the contract allow termination, not just damages.
Check whether time is stated to be of the essence for key dates.
Estimate your damages on a breach, with mitigation built in.
Gather evidence of why the site is unique if specific performance may matter.
Test any liquidated damages figure against a genuine estimate of loss.
Follow the notice and cure process exactly before terminating.
Take advice before sending any message that ends a contract.
head: Field checklist
speak: A breach is a failure to perform, actual or anticipated, and it can be minor or serious. A minor breach gives damages; a serious one may also let you terminate. Damages aim to put me where performance would have put me, limited by mitigation, so I must reasonably reduce my loss, and by remoteness, so only foreseeable losses count. If a seller refuses to close at 2 million and I must pay 2.3 for a similar site, my basic loss is the 300,000 difference plus wasted costs. Because land is treated as unique, a court may order specific performance, but that is discretionary. Contracts can price breach in advance with deposits and liquidated damages, enforceable if they are genuine estimates rather than penalties. I terminate only with a clear right and by the contract's notice process, never in an angry email.
terms: Mitigation — the innocent party's duty to take reasonable steps to reduce its loss after a breach.
Specific performance — a court order requiring a party to perform its contract, available for land at the court's discretion.
Liquidated damages — a sum agreed in advance as compensation for a defined breach, unenforceable in many systems if it is a penalty.

hostile.q: The buyer of a unit has defaulted. Your sales agent says hold out for full price and sue for the difference. Why not?
hostile.a: Because the law expects us to mitigate. If we refuse reasonable offers while waiting for full price, a court may cut our claim by whatever we could have avoided. We will relist at the current market price, document every offer and carrying cost, keep the deposit if the contract and local law allow, and claim any shortfall above it. Our lawyer will confirm the notice steps before we treat the contract as ended.

title: Working back from the worst day: deposits and liquidated damages
summary: Instead of accepting a market-standard deposit or delay figure, start from the loss you would suffer on the bad day and work backward to the number the contract needs. This lesson sizes a pre-sale deposit from a resale shortfall, a land deposit from your own loss limit, and a daily liquidated damages figure from carrying cost, all with hypothetical round numbers.
body:
Mr Shabazz, most people set deposits and delay damages by asking what is normal. A lender sets them by asking what the bad day costs and working backward. Do it that way and every number in your contract has a reason you can defend in a negotiation and, if it comes to it, in front of a judge.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: what two limits apply to contract damages?

A. Mitigation, meaning the innocent party must reasonably reduce its loss, and remoteness, meaning only losses reasonably foreseeable when the contract was made are generally recoverable.

Q. From the money checkpoint: what is peak funding?

A. The point where a project's cumulative cash outflow is largest, usually near completion. It sizes the interest reserve and the money that must be in place before any comes back.

Q. From the owner accounting week: what does capitalising interest during construction do to reported profit?

A. It keeps the interest off the income statement while the building is being built, adding it to the cost of the asset instead. The cash is still paid, or added to the loan, so profit and cash diverge.

Why this matters

A deposit that is too small leaves you carrying the loss when a buyer walks. One that is too large may be challenged as a penalty, or may simply drive buyers away. A delay figure that is too low lets a contractor finish late cheaply; one that is plainly punitive may not be enforced. The way to land in the right place is to begin with the outcome you are protecting against and solve for the clause.

Worked example one: sizing a pre-sale deposit from the resale shortfall

The finished outcome we start from: a buyer of a pre-sold condominium unit defaults at completion, and you must resell into a weaker market. All numbers hypothetical. The unit is sold for $500,000.

Step 1: Price the market fall you want to survive. You decide to protect against a 15 percent fall in resale price by completion, which is your downside case, not a forecast. That is $75,000.

Step 2: Add resale costs. Commission, legal and marketing on a resale at, say, 3 percent of $425,000 is about $12,750. Round to $13,000.

Step 3: Add carrying cost while you resell. If it takes three months to resell and the unit's share of loan interest, taxes, insurance and common charges is about $2,000 a month, that is $6,000.

Step 4: Total the loss. $75,000 plus $13,000 plus $6,000 is $94,000.

Step 5: Convert to a deposit. $94,000 divided by $500,000 is about 19 percent. So a deposit of roughly 20 percent covers your downside case on a single default. A 10 percent deposit covers only about half of it.

Then the reality check. Whether you can require or keep a deposit of that size, how it must be held, and whether part must be held in trust or insured, depend on consumer protection and real estate laws that vary by place; that is the subject of a later week on condominium pre-sales. And lenders often set their own pre-sale deposit requirements as a commercial practice. The calculation does not override those rules; it tells you what level of protection you are trading away when you accept less.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: sizing your own land deposit from your loss limit

Now you are the buyer. The finished outcome we start from: the deal fails after you are committed, and you lose money. Start with the most you can lose on this deal without breaching your liquidity floor. Suppose that is $150,000.

Step 1: Subtract costs you will spend whatever happens. Diligence, legal and design work before waiver are estimated at $60,000. That leaves $90,000 of capacity for money at risk.

Step 2: Work out the most deposit you can put at risk before waiver. Any deposit that is non-refundable before you waive conditions must fit inside $90,000. So a $50,000 refundable deposit on signing is acceptable, and a $200,000 non-refundable one is not.

Step 3: Work out what changes at waiver. After waiver the deposit is typically at risk, and your remaining exposure is the deposit plus any claim beyond it if you then default. If the seller wants $200,000 on waiver, you must be certain enough of closing at waiver that losing $200,000 is outside your realistic cases. That certainty is what the diligence period is for. If you cannot reach it in the period offered, the period is too short, not the deposit too high.

So the backward method produces a negotiating position with reasons: "We can offer $50,000 refundable until waiver at day 45, then $150,000 more, non-refundable, because that is when our diligence will be complete."

Worked example three: a daily liquidated damages figure from carrying cost

The finished outcome: the contractor finishes 60 days late. What does each day cost you? Start from the costs that delay actually causes.

Step 1: Interest. A $15,000,000 drawn loan at 7 percent costs $1,050,000 a year, about $2,880 a day.

Step 2: Lost income. A building forecast to earn $1,600,000 of net operating income a year loses about $4,380 a day of NOI for each day it opens late, once it would have been earning.

Step 3: Your own overhead and fees. Project management, insurance extension and consultants staying on site, say $740 a day.

Step 4: Total. About $2,880 plus $4,380 plus $740, which is $8,000 a day. Sixty days late is about $480,000.

That figure is your genuine pre-estimate of loss, which in many common-law systems is what makes a liquidated damages clause defensible rather than a penalty. You may still agree a lower figure, or a cap, in exchange for a lower price or a stronger schedule commitment; contractors price this risk. But if you agree $1,000 a day, you know you are absorbing about $7,000 a day yourself, and you can tell your lender and investors exactly that. Verify the enforceability test against current law where the contract will be enforced.

Cross-check: do the three numbers fit together?

Run them against each other. If the contractor is 60 days late, your completion slips 60 days, and your pre-sale buyers close 60 days later in whatever market exists then. A late building therefore raises the chance of buyer defaults at the same moment it raises your interest bill. The delay figure you agree with the contractor, the deposits you take from buyers and your own loss limit are one system, not three separate clauses. Write them on one page, with the bad day each one protects, and check that the worst realistic combination still fits inside your reserves.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is copying market-standard figures without knowing what they protect. A 10 percent deposit or a round daily figure may be normal and still leave a large part of your downside uncovered. The control is to work every protective number backward from a named bad day, write the calculation in the deal file, and record any gap you accept as a known cost.

The beginner's mistake

Setting liquidated damages as high as possible to scare the contractor. A figure far above any genuine estimate of loss is the shape a court may treat as a penalty, and contractors simply add the risk to their price. Accurate beats aggressive.

Callback

In the money checkpoint, Sage worked backward from a required return to the most you could pay for land. Today is the same method aimed at protection: start from the outcome you must survive, walk back through each cost, and the clause is what is left. The backward method works on every number that has a reason behind it.

Recap

A pre-sale deposit sized from a 15 percent fall, resale costs and carrying cost comes to about 19 percent here. Your own land deposit fits inside your loss limit after fixed costs. A daily delay figure built from interest, lost income and overhead comes to about $8,000. Work every protective number back from the bad day and record any gap you accept.

Next: JAX, in the room with a seller who wants a binding letter of intent.
checklist: Name the bad day each protective clause is meant to cover.
Size pre-sale deposits from resale fall, resale costs and carrying cost.
Fit your own non-refundable deposits inside your loss limit after fixed costs.
Match the diligence period to the certainty you need before waiver.
Build liquidated damages from interest, lost income and overhead per day.
Record any gap between the agreed figure and your true loss as a known cost.
Check deposit, trust and penalty rules where the contract will be enforced.
head: Field checklist
speak: I size protective clauses backward from the bad day. For a pre-sold unit at 500,000, if I want to survive a 15 percent fall, that is 75,000, plus about 13,000 of resale costs and 6,000 of carrying cost: 94,000, or about 19 percent of the price. A 10 percent deposit covers only half of that, so I know the gap I am accepting, subject to local deposit and consumer rules. As a buyer, I start from the most I can lose, subtract the costs I will spend anyway, and fit any non-refundable deposit before waiver inside what is left. For contractor delay, I add interest of about 2,880 a day, lost NOI of about 4,380 and overhead of about 740: roughly 8,000 a day. That is a genuine pre-estimate of loss, which is what makes liquidated damages defensible, and if I accept less I record the difference as a known cost.
terms: Pre-estimate of loss — a reasoned forecast, made when the contract is signed, of the loss a defined breach would cause.
Carrying cost — the cost of holding an asset over time, such as interest, taxes, insurance and charges.
Loss limit — the most you have decided you can lose on one deal without breaching your liquidity floor.

hostile.q: Every other developer in this market takes a 10 percent deposit. Why are you asking buyers for 20 and scaring them off?
hostile.a: Because on our downside case a single default costs about 94,000 on a 500,000 unit, roughly 19 percent: a 15 percent price fall, resale costs and three months of carrying cost. At 10 percent we absorb about half of that ourselves on every default. We are prepared to stage the deposit across construction to make it easier to pay, and we will comply with whatever the local rules require on how it is held. But I would rather sell fewer units to committed buyers than carry their downside for them.

title: The seller who wants the letter of intent to bind
summary: A landowner wants your letter of intent to be binding on price so you cannot walk away or retrade. This lesson scripts the meeting: what the seller really fears, how to offer certainty without being bound before diligence, which clauses should bind, the lines never to say and how to hold your state when the seller threatens to go elsewhere.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when a seller asks for a binding letter of intent, the request is rarely about law. It is about fear: of being tied up, then dropped or squeezed on price. Answer the fear with specific commitments, and you can keep the price non-binding until your diligence is done.

Recall

Q. From yesterday: how do you size a daily liquidated damages figure?

A. From the costs a day of delay actually causes: interest on the drawn loan, lost net operating income and your own overhead. That gives a genuine pre-estimate of loss.

Q. From the money checkpoint: what should you lead with in an investment committee?

A. The request, the bottom line and the stress-case result, then the spread rather than the IRR.

Q. From the owner accounting week: why does an owner report work in progress separately from finished assets?

A. Because its value rests on estimates of how far along the work is and what it will cost to finish. Keeping it separate shows readers which part of the balance sheet is still a judgement.

Why this matters

Rule 20 says every letter of intent states which clauses bind and which do not, and that nothing else binds until signature. A seller who has been burned before may push hard against that. If you give in, you may be bound to a price before you know what is under the ground. If you refuse flatly, you may lose the site. The skill is to give the seller enough certainty to say yes without giving away the right to walk.

The scene

This is a composite scene with hypothetical numbers. Mrs Alvarez owns a 2,000 square metre lot. You have agreed $2,000,000 in principle. Her lawyer has sent a draft letter of intent that says the price and closing date are binding on signing, with no conditions, and that you pay $100,000 non-refundable on signature. She tells you, across her kitchen table: "Last time a developer tied me up for six months, then cut his offer by a third the week before closing. I won't do that again."

The question behind the question

When she says "binding," the question behind it is: "How do I know you won't waste my time and then retrade?" When she asks for $100,000 non-refundable, the question behind it is: "What does it cost you to walk away?" She is not asking for a legal concept; she is asking for skin in the game and a clock.

The lines to say

Acknowledge first: "That sounds like it cost you real money and six months. I'd be wary too."

Then offer specific protection against what happened to her: "Here's what I can commit to in writing. I'll do my diligence in 45 days, not six months. I'll pay $25,000 on signing for that exclusivity, and it's yours whatever happens. If I walk, I'll give you every report I've paid for, so the next buyer starts ahead. And I'll put in the letter that the only grounds for me to walk or change the price are specific findings: contamination, a title problem, or zoning that doesn't allow the 60 units we've discussed."

Then explain what must stay non-binding, and why: "What I can't do is bind myself to the price before I know what's under the ground. No lender will fund me if I do, and it wouldn't protect you anyway, because a buyer who can't close can't pay."

Say that out loud now.

Worked example: the numbers you carry into the room

From the money lesson this week, you know the diligence condition is worth about $150,000 to you on your own estimate: a 25 percent chance of a finding that takes $600,000 off the land's value. So binding the price now would cost you that much in expected value. A $25,000 non-refundable exclusivity fee is a small fraction of it, and it compensates her directly for the 45 days of her time.

You also know your carrying cost while the deal is live is about $15,000 a month, so a 45-day period costs you roughly $22,500. Offering speed is not a concession; it saves you money too. Present it as what it is: a commitment that costs both of you less.

If she pushes for more, you have a trade ready: "If you'd like more certainty, I'll put $150,000 on deposit when I waive conditions at day 45, non-refundable from then. At that point I'll have done the work, and the price binds."

Which clauses should bind

In the letter itself, state in the first paragraph that only these clauses bind: exclusivity for 45 days and the $25,000 fee; confidentiality; your obligation to share reports if you walk; each side paying its own costs; and governing law. Everything else, including price, closing date and deposit, binds only when the definitive agreement is signed. That is Rule 20 turned into a document she can read.

The lines never to say

Never say "Trust me" or "My word is good." She has heard it before, from the developer who cut his price. Never say "That's standard" about anything she objects to; it dismisses her experience. Never say "My lawyer won't let me," which makes you look like you have no authority. Never hint that you might pay more later if she signs now. And never criticise the previous developer by name; she may know him, and it sounds like you are next.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after she describes what happened last time. Let her finish, then pause before you answer; rushing to reassure tells her you did not listen. Stay silent after you lay out your offer, the 45 days, the fee, the reports and the specific grounds. Let her or her lawyer respond. The first person to fill that silence usually concedes something.

Holding your state

She may say: "Then I'll sell to someone who will sign binding." Your body will want to give ground. Breathe out slowly before you answer, a practitioner habit with research behind it, done sitting still. Then: "That might be the right choice for you, and if they can close, I'd understand. If they can't, I'll still be here at $2,000,000, with 45 days of diligence and $25,000 you keep." Holding your terms calmly, without heat, is more persuasive than any argument, because it shows you have a walk-away and are not bluffing.

After the meeting

Send a short email the same day summarising what you offered, with Rule 20's not-an-offer sentence at the top so the summary itself does not form a contract. Ask your lawyer to turn it into a letter of intent with the binding and non-binding clauses separated as agreed. Log the date you offered 45 days, so you hold yourself to it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a binding price to win the site, then discovering a problem you are already committed to pay for. The control is never to bind the price before diligence; instead, bind your behaviour: a short period, a fee she keeps, reports she gets, and written grounds for walking.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing the law. Telling her that letters of intent are usually non-binding answers the wrong question. She knows what she wants; she wants protection against being strung along. Give her that in specific, measurable promises, and the legal form stops mattering to her.

Callback

In the communication weeks you learned acknowledge, bridge, answer. Mrs Alvarez's demand is a hostile question in disguise: "Why should I trust you?" Acknowledge her experience, bridge to what you can commit to, and answer with a number and a date. The structure is the same whether the questioner is a lender or a landowner at her kitchen table.

Recap

A seller who wants a binding letter fears being tied up and squeezed. Answer that with a short diligence period, a fee she keeps, reports she receives and written grounds for walking. Keep the price non-binding until waiver, then commit a larger deposit. Put the binding clauses in the first paragraph, and confirm everything in writing the same day.

Next: Kema, with the week's six questions, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a letter of intent, and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Find the fear behind a request for a binding letter of intent.
Offer a short, dated diligence period instead of a binding price.
Pay a modest exclusivity fee the seller keeps whatever happens.
Promise to share your reports if you walk away.
Write down the specific findings that allow you to walk or reprice.
List the binding clauses in the first paragraph; keep price non-binding until signature.
Confirm the meeting in writing the same day, with a not-an-offer statement.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a seller wants a binding letter of intent, she is afraid of being tied up and then squeezed on price. I acknowledge that, then offer specific protection instead of a binding price: 45 days of diligence, not six months; a 25,000 dollar exclusivity fee she keeps whatever happens; every report I paid for if I walk; and written grounds, such as contamination, title or zoning, as the only reasons to walk or reprice. I explain that I cannot bind the price before diligence, because no lender would fund it and a buyer who cannot close cannot pay. If she wants more, I offer a larger deposit, non-refundable at waiver. The letter's first paragraph lists the binding clauses: exclusivity, the fee, confidentiality, reports, costs and governing law. Everything else binds only on signature. I never say trust me, and I confirm everything in writing the same day.
terms: Binding clause — a provision of a letter of intent that the parties intend to be enforceable immediately, such as exclusivity or confidentiality.
Exclusivity fee — a payment to a seller in return for not dealing with other buyers for a set period.
Walk right — a buyer's right to end a deal before waiver on stated grounds, such as an adverse diligence finding.

hostile.q: If you're serious, sign the price as binding today. Anyone who won't is planning to cut it later. Isn't that what you're doing?
hostile.a: No, and I'll put that in writing. The only grounds on which I can walk or change the price are specific findings in the next 45 days: contamination, a title defect, or zoning that does not allow the units we discussed. If none of those appears, I close at 2 million. You keep the 25,000 fee whatever happens, and you get every report I pay for. Binding the price today would not protect you more, because no lender will fund a site that has not been checked.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Contracts: quiz, Auditor's Chair and boardroom
summary: Six questions test the week: formation, counter-offers, conditions, what binds in a letter of intent, remedies and Rule 20. Cole's Auditor's Chair reads a hypothetical letter of intent the way a hostile auditor would and finds eight defects. The boardroom drill asks for the week in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week taught you to see the moment a promise becomes enforceable, and to decide in advance what each promise costs if it is broken. Today we check that you can spot both on a page you did not write.

Recall

Q. From the money checkpoint: what is the development spread?

A. Yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin you are paid for taking development risk.

Q. From last week: why does a contract need to name its governing law and forum?

A. So that when there is a dispute, both sides know which rules apply and which court or tribunal decides, instead of fighting first about where to fight.

Q. From the owner accounting week: what is the difference between accrual and cash accounting?

A. Accrual records revenue when earned and costs when incurred; cash records them when money moves.

Why this matters

You will read more contracts than you draft. Lawyers draft; developers decide whether to sign. The habit you need is a fast, structured reading that finds what binds, when it binds, what you get if it breaks, and where you could be bound by accident.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the elements of contract formation in the common-law tradition.

Answer: An offer, an acceptance that matches it exactly, consideration from each side, an intention to be legally bound, and terms certain enough to enforce. Some contracts, including many for land, must also be in signed writing.

Question 2. You offer $2,000,000 closing in 90 days. The owner replies "Yes, but 60 days." You reply "Fine." What has happened?

Answer: Her reply was a counter-offer that rejected your original offer. Your "Fine" may have accepted it, forming a contract at $2,000,000 with a 60-day close, subject to any writing requirement for land contracts. The control is a not-an-offer statement on every pre-contract message.

Question 3. What should every condition precedent state?

Answer: The event, the standard for satisfying it, who decides, the deadline, how notice is given, and what happens if it fails, including what happens to the deposit.

Question 4. What usually binds in a well-drafted letter of intent?

Answer: Exclusivity, confidentiality, costs, governing law and sometimes a fee; everything else, including price, binds only when the definitive agreement is signed. The first paragraph should say so.

Question 5. A seller refuses to close at $2,000,000 and you buy a similar site for $2,300,000, spending $30,000 more on diligence. What is your basic loss, and what limits it?

Answer: About $330,000. It is limited by mitigation, so you must act reasonably to reduce it, and by remoteness, so a claim for lost development profit faces the foreseeability and certainty tests.

Question 6. What is Rule 20?

Answer: Every letter of intent I sign or receive states, in its first paragraph, which clauses bind and which do not; I never announce, act on or let anyone treat a deal as agreed until the definitive agreement is signed, and I never step into a deal without written confirmation that no one else holds a binding agreement.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

LEX set out how a promise becomes a contract and how conditions decide when it bites. Ford and Cole showed, through Pennzoil and Texaco, how an agreement in principle and an announcement became a verdict of more than ten billion dollars. JAX priced a condition, a deposit and exclusivity in money. LEX explained breach, damages, specific performance and the penalty rule. Roman worked backward from the worst day to a deposit and a daily delay figure. JAX sat at a seller's kitchen table and kept the price non-binding while answering her fear.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Every fourth week the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: you read a hypothetical document as a hostile auditor would, looking for what is missing, inconsistent or convenient. Here is a one-page letter of intent a developer has signed.

"Letter of intent. The Buyer agrees to purchase the Property for $2,000,000. A deposit of $200,000 is payable on signing. The Buyer may terminate if it is not satisfied with its due diligence. The Seller will not market the Property during the due diligence period. Closing will occur on a date to be agreed. The parties will negotiate in good faith a purchase agreement on customary terms. The Buyer has advised its investors that the site has been acquired. Signed by the Buyer only."

Read it once more as the auditor. Then compare with the defects below.

  1. There is no statement of which clauses bind and which do not. Under Rule 20, its first paragraph should say so. As written, a court could find the price binding.
  2. "The Buyer agrees to purchase" is language of commitment, not of intention. A non-binding letter should say the parties intend to negotiate.
  3. The $200,000 deposit has no refund terms, no holder and no link to the diligence condition, so it is unclear whether the buyer gets it back on walking.
  4. "If it is not satisfied" has no deadline, no notice method and no standard. Is satisfaction in the buyer's sole discretion, or must it be reasonable?
  5. Exclusivity runs for "the due diligence period," which is never defined, so its length is unknown.
  6. "A date to be agreed" leaves an essential term open, which can make a contract uncertain and can also leave the buyer with no fixed timetable.
  7. "Customary terms" and good faith negotiation are undefined, and in some systems a good faith obligation can itself be enforceable.
  8. The buyer has told investors the site "has been acquired." That is a statement of fact that is false, a misrepresentation risk to the investors, and conduct a court might read as treating the deal as done. And the letter is signed by one party only.

The auditor's conclusion would be blunt: this document may bind the buyer to a price with no clear way out, while giving the seller almost nothing firm, and the buyer's own investor update has created a second problem. Rewrite it, and correct the investor update today.

The boardroom drill

Stand up, set a two-minute timer, and explain this week to a board that has never read a contract. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "A contract is a promise the law will enforce. It forms when an offer is accepted without changes, each side gives something, both intend to be bound and the terms are clear. That can happen in an email chain, so every pre-contract message we send says it is not an offer. Conditions let us buy land without being bound until diligence is done, and each one has a deadline, a standard and a consequence. Letters of intent are where most accidental commitments happen, so ours list the binding clauses, exclusivity, confidentiality and costs, in the first paragraph, and say the price binds only when the full agreement is signed. If the other side breaks a contract, the default remedy is money that puts us where performance would have, reduced by anything we could reasonably have avoided. We set deposits and delay figures by working back from what the bad day would cost us. That is our Rule 20."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is reading a preliminary document as if its label decided its effect. "Letter of intent" on the heading binds no one and frees no one; the words and the conduct do. The control is the Auditor's Chair reading, every time, before you sign.

The beginner's mistake

Reading contracts front to back like a story. Read them by question: what binds, when, what happens if it breaks, and how notice is given. Find each answer, mark it, and anything you cannot find is the defect.

Callback

Two weeks ago, at the money checkpoint, LEX taught that every number you hand over is a promise of some kind. This week completes that thought: every promise has a moment when it becomes enforceable and a price when it is broken. The investor update in today's drill shows both lessons failing at once.

Recap

Formation, counter-offers, conditions, binding and non-binding clauses, remedies and Rule 20. Answer the six questions aloud once more and practise the boardroom drill before you close the app.

head: The six questions
speak: A contract is a set of promises the law will enforce. In common-law systems it forms with an offer, an acceptance that matches it exactly, consideration from each side, an intention to be bound and certain terms, and land contracts often need signed writing too. A reply that changes a term is a counter-offer, so an email chain can bind me by accident unless I state it is not an offer. Conditions decide when obligations bite, and each needs an event, a standard, a decider, a deadline, a notice method and a consequence. Pennzoil and Texaco showed that an agreement in principle plus conduct can be found binding. If the other side breaches, damages aim to put me where performance would have, limited by mitigation and foreseeability. I price deposits and delay figures from the bad day. Rule 20: every letter of intent says up front what binds and what does not.
terms: Counter-offer — a reply that changes an offer's terms, rejecting it and making a new offer.
Condition precedent — an event that must happen before an obligation, or the contract, takes effect.
Good faith obligation — a duty to negotiate or perform honestly, which in some systems can itself be enforceable.

hostile.q: Your letter of intent says the buyer agrees to purchase for 2 million and your investor update says the site is acquired. Are you bound or not?
hostile.a: We may be, and I will not pretend otherwise. I have asked our lawyer to review the letter's wording and our conduct today. I am correcting the investor update now to say we have signed a letter of intent and are in diligence, not that we have acquired the site. From here, the definitive agreement will carry clear conditions and deadlines, and every future letter will list its binding clauses in the first paragraph.
